Christmas Presents Until the End of Time?

 “So, do you think it’ll go? Do you think they’ll sell?” Mike Moffat asked, looking at the first assembled Asgard on the engineering bench in my garage. He was being Mike-fidgety, rocking from heel to heel in the small, chilly space. 

 “Well, on paper it looks good,” I told him. “But you know how that works. They’ll either sell, or we’ll have Christmas presents until the end of time.”

 Mike laughed, a little nervously. Because he knew how it goes. You can plan and study, do endless market research and cost studies, run focus groups and get tons of input from key prospects and do all the little things that companies do to procrastinate and dither and second-guess before putting out another “gotta have” product…and things can still go sideways. 

 But this isn’t a story about stuff like that. This is a story about gut feelings, good guesses, and not following the herd. And succeeding. 

 This is the story of Schiit Audio, the world’s most improbable start-up.

 Yes. Schiit. Let’s start with that as an improbability factor. What company in its right mind would name itself that? I mean, if you were a marketing agency and proposed that name to a client, how would they react? You’d be picking your butt up off the pavement outside their headquarters, post-haste. 

 But that isn’t all that made us a crap candidate for succeeding. Consider:
• We started this with no outside funds, no VC, no crowdfunding
• We’d both been out of audio for about 15+ years—more on that later
• We went with direct sales, even though that had only really worked for one other company—Emotiva
• We started with no staff, in my garage
• We decided to make everything in the USA, even though the prevailing wisdom of the time was “China’s the World’s Manufacturing Floor, why even try to compete?”
• And, in a complete burst of insanity, we decided to start with inexpensive products

 Ah, and it’s now probably past time I introduce myself. I’m Jason Stoddard, Co-Founder of Schiit Audio. Mike Moffat’s my business partner. Our official titles are “Head” and “Number 2” respectively. Hey, Mike asked for it. No, we don’t take ourselves too seriously here. 

 I won’t bore you with our full CVs (that’s fancy-speak for wut we dun), but you may have heard of Mike Moffat. He was the founder of Theta (the first one, the analog one), in the late 1970s. You can blame him, at least in part, for resurrecting tube audio. He was the first person to use 6DJ8s in audio. He installed Philip K. Dick’s stereo systems. He sold amps to L. Ron Hubbard (no, you can’t make this schiit up). Then, in the 1980s, he became the Father of the DAC with Theta Digital. His DSPre was the first standalone DAC on the market, and it was a showstopper—its own digital filter algorithms running on Motorola DSPs so powerful they couldn’t be exported into the Soviet Union, for a start. Theta mopped up in the DAC world for several years, then Mike founded Angstrom, the maker of the world’s first upgradable surround processor. From there, Mike moved into entertainment, creating complex systems for digital movie distribution. At least until I tempted him away with Schiit.

 I’m…well, I’m confused. I’m a published, award-winning science fiction author (strangeandhappy.com), a summa cum laude BS Engineering analog geek (schiit.com) and 20-year veteran of the marketing wars at another company I founded (centric.com). I’ve done stuff as strange as lecture Harvard professors on virtual world marketing, and as driven as earning my way to Vice-President, Engineering at Sumo at age 25, which nominally made me Ed Miller’s boss—he was the founder of Souncraftsmen, Sherwood and Great American Sound, and head of engineering for SAE, to drop some names. Not that Ed cared, he just did his own thing. He was cool.

 I’m the one writing this book. You can blame it all on me. I have no illusions of this being a best-seller, or of it changing the world. But I think we have an interesting story—one that others can learn from, both in and out of audio.

 “Oh yeah?” you ask, leaning back and crossing your arms. “Well, I ain’t gonna read no sixty thousand words about some small-time company just to get few phrases that belong on Sucksessories posters.”

 Cool. Gotcha. So I’ll cut to the chase. If you’re only interested in business intelligence, you won’t have to read any further than the next 7 bullet points:
1. Shooting to be the next billion-dollar mass-market company is insane—you might as well buy lottery tickets.
2. Niche is where it’s at—specifically a niche where people can get in fistfights over the color of a knob.
3. Pick a niche you know and love and do something nobody else can do—"me-too" never works.
4. Be memorable—this isn’t about getting 
everyone 
to 
like
 you, this is about getting 
some
 people to 
love
 you.
5. Go direct—distribution is a poisonous remnant of 19th century economics in a disintermediated world.
6. Run from both conventional marketing wisdom and the social media mavens—both of them are geared towards the mass market with eight-digit ad budgets and multiple decades to build a brand. 
7. Don’t think this'll be easy—this is hard work, but you’ll also be having a whole lot of fun if you’re doing it right!

 Okay, now you’re skeptical. You’re thinking: But I just read a book from (insert the name of some multibillion-dollar-valuation corporate CEO here), and he said it’s easy to reach the masses and change the world, and it seems like anyone can do it, why would I shoot for less than that?

 That’s cool. That is, if you’re lucky enough to come up with something different enough to merit venture funding, if you get through all the rounds with the team and product intact, if something better doesn’t come out of nowhere, if the public whims don’t change, if you don’t get ousted before the real money starts, if you’re cool with 100 hour weeks and lots of travel and losing touch with the real fun of creation and becoming a new salesman with his dog-and-pony show for the money guys in Silly Valley or Singapore or wherever the money is in this moment, more power to you. Go ahead and create the next Amazon, Apple, Facebook, or Google. This book isn’t for you, and you can stop reading now.

 But I have a lot of friends who have gone down that route. Brilliant people. Hard workers. They don’t have any problem with all of the above. They go even farther, begging and scraping to keep the team stapled together when the money gets thin, mortgaging everything they have on the One Big Idea…

 …and doing it again when the first one doesn’t get past angel funding. 

 …and doing it again when the second one doesn’t get its second round.

 …and doing it again and again and again, as many times as it takes.

 Bottom line, there are plenty of billion-dollar ideas out there. Making one into a real company that succeeds isn’t just a lot of work. It’s about money, luck, connections, money, luck, money, and luck. And more luck.

 This story is for people who don’t have a lot of the above. For people who are shooting to create a company that might do a million a year, or ten million, or maybe a hundred million, eventually, way out in the future.

 So, if you’d like to know more about where we came from, how we got started, why the crazy name, where the fixation on Norse mythology came from, our first successes, our first failures, what we screwed up later (hell, if you buy anything from us after reading how much we mess things up, it’ll be a minor miracle), how we develop products and market and go to shows and work with suppliers and do everything in the USA except the Magni wall-wart, and about ten thousand other things, read on. 

 If you’re looking for a story that will make you an instant millionaire, cure cancer, repel an alien invasion, or thwart the plans of an evil CEO to turn the world into a dystopic corpocrat future, you’ve come to the wrong place.

 Oh, and about those Asgard Christmas presents? 

 To date, we haven’t had to give a single one away. In fact, staying in stock through the holidays is one of the hardest things to do around here. Yes. Even 42 months later.

 And with that, let’s flash back 20+ years…

For years, MOONDROP has charted the unexplored frontiers of HiFi audio – from the boundary-breaking Aria’s meteoric rise as the gateway to high-fidelity sound, to professional over-ear headphones that redefined the studio. Today, they turn the page and introduce the 
Horizon 
– a revolutionary addition to MOONDROP's headphone lineup!

The Horizon represents a new benchmark in MOONDROP's professional over-ear headphones lineup. It leverages cutting-edge technology and a completely new structural design to achieve ultra-low distortion and high energy conversion efficiency that surpasses its predecessors.

Unlike planar headphones, the Horizon utilizes a dynamic driver that theoretically achieves higher efficiency through systematic engineering, thereby reducing the driving threshold. Additionally, its lightweight design enhances the listening experience, allowing users to enjoy high-resolution, low-distortion HiFi sound quality across a broader range of use cases.

The Horizon features MOONDROP’s latest generation of high-performance 50mm ULT dynamic driver. After two years of extensive research, development, and optimization, we have significantly improved the dynamic range, reduced distortion, and expanded the bandwidth, achieving leading levels compared to previous products.

The effective magnetic flux density in the magnetic gap reaches an impressive 1.85T. Utilizing Comsol, a large-scale finite element simulation system, we’ve been able to overcome the limitations of traditional experimentation. This allows us to conduct numerous simulations and optimizations on the magnetic circuit and structure of the driver, enhancing the dynamic driver performance to the fullest extent within current technological capabilities.

This dynamic driver incorporates two sets of N55 Nd magnets, each with a natural flux exceeding 1.6T. Through advanced magnetic circuit optimization design, we've further enhanced the magnetic gap flux density to 1.85T, while ensuring uniformity across the entire magnetic gap.

To achieve treble extension in the diaphragm of a 50mm large-sized driver, it is essential to balance rigidity and damping. After extensive simulation calculations of material characteristics and over ten optimization experiments with diaphragm samples, we have ultimately selected a diaphragm material that fulfills the requirements for long stroke, full frequency response, and low nonlinearity.

PEN material, commonly used in traditional flagship headphone dynamic drivers, offers excellent rigidity and good damping characteristics for the dome. The titanium plating process enhances the surface sound speed, further reducing split vibrations.

The liquid silica gel suspension differs from traditional methods, requiring ultra-thin materials to be direct-injection molded using high-precision molds. Compared to standard suspensions, it provides higher reliability at larger amplitudes, and its supporting and damping characteristics are improved through double-layer composite technology.

To create a wider soundstage and ensure complete auricle coupling for an enhanced listening experience, the Horizon features a newly designed large-angle driver inclined structure. This design allows sound waves radiated by the driver to travel a more complete path, arriving from the oblique front. This not only facilitates auricle coupling but also promotes natural diffusion at various angles through a high sound transmission structure.

As a result, the Horizon offers a wider soundstage and a more natural timbre compared to traditional dynamic headphones.

The frequency response characteristics of Horizon align with the VDSF standard, thanks to the newly designed 50mm ULT dynamic driver. With a free-field f0 as low as 80Hz, it delivers sub-bass performance that is rare in open dynamic driver headphones, while also providing smooth high-frequency responses typical of larger dynamic drivers. This results in punchy dynamics and a laid-back sound profile.

Thanks to the innovative driver structure and diaphragm material used in the brand-new 50mm ULT dynamic driver, the Horizon headphones achieve ultra-low nonlinear distortion, making them stand out among dynamic driver headphones. This design allows for clearer and more accurate reproduction of sound details.

With its high-performance magnetic circuit, even a large composite diaphragm can be easily driven. The Horizon can be powered by an integrated sound card from a computer or a portable device, making it suitable for gaming. When connected to a powerful desktop amplifier, it can unlock even greater performance capabilities.

The 
Horizon
 includes the widely used and reliable dual 3.5mm interchangeable cable that allows users to easily replace cables to accommodate various usage scenarios, and comes with a 4.4mm balanced cable that features a four-strand arrangement, made from high-quality 6N purity copper provided by FURUKAWA. The parallel arrangement structure is designed to minimize interference and ensure optimal signal transmission quality.

Master Tuned version of the iDSD GR2 reimagined through the ears of Grammy and Brit Award-winning producer Steve Levine
Southport, UK, October 1, 2026–– 
iFi Audio
, a British pioneer in audio innovation, has announced the launch of the iDSD GR2 MT, a Master Tuned version of its acclaimed iDSD GR2 portable DAC/amp. Reimagined through the ears of Grammy and Brit Award-winning producer Steve Levine, the GR2 MT pairs component-level upgrades with two exclusive, Levine-voiced digital filters to deliver the balance and emotional potency that defines his signature sound. Every sonic decision was guided by Levine himself; it is the sound of a lifetime of studio experience and critical listening.

Steve Levine is a celebrated British record producer whose credits span genres and generations, from Culture Club and the Beach Boys to Gary Moore, Ziggy Marley, and Lemmy and Motorhead. His contribution to music has earned him a number of prestigious industry honours, including a Brit Award, a Musicweek Award, and a Grammy for his work with Deniece Williams. Today, Levine continues to produce exciting new talent from his studio in the heart of Liverpool's Baltic Triangle, including artists signed to his own label, Baltic Jazz Records.

“The goal of any producer is to document the authenticity and emotion behind the artist’s performance,” says Levine. “I have voiced the iDSD GR2 MT with this same goal in mind, and I hope you feel that when you listen”.
Key Upgrades

The GR2 MT builds on the standard GR2 with a series of component-level upgrades. Its high-resolution touch colour display now carries an illuminated silkscreen logo, while the standard FR-4 circuit board is replaced with an aerospace-grade hydrocarbon ceramic PCB offering near-zero signal loss.

The GR2’s OVA2637 with standard surface-mount resistors DAC I/V stage is replaced with OV4627A with audiophile-grade tantalum resistors, and the amp stage moves from standard electrolytic capacitors to Audio Note Kaisei capacitors.

As with its predecessor, at the core of the iDSD GR2 MT is the Burr-Brown PCM1795 DAC, fitted with Levine’s two exclusive filters, alongside JVCKENWOOD’s K2HD Technology, which recovers the depth and nuance of master recordings. The device delivers over 1,500mW RMS power output at 32 ohms, driven through an TFT-LCD display with capacitive touchscreen control.

Wireless listeners are served by Bluetooth 5.4 with aptX Lossless and LDAC, enabling CD-quality playback with no data loss. Hybrid power modes are designed to maximise battery lifespan, connectivity spans both digital and analogue options, and the GR2 MT is fully compatible with the iFi Nexis app for over-the-air updates and advanced control.

besides the Battery Health Mode issue for which I currently have an open ticket
. Sound‑wise and feature‑wise, it’s been a fantastic device: great power, stable Bluetooth, excellent touchscreen UI, K2/K2HD, and a warm, cinematic tuning that works beautifully with my IEMs. But after reading through the specs of the new GR2 MT, I have to be honest: I’m annoyed at how iFi handled this release.

The GR2 MT is being marketed as a “Master Tuned” studio‑approved version, but when you actually compare the specs side‑by‑side, it becomes very clear what this really is: 
a GR2 with a refined analogue stage, two extra filters, and a cosmetic upgrade - not a new generation.

Here’s the breakdown:
Both GR2 and GR2 MT have:
Burr‑Brown PCM1795 DAC
OLED colour capacitive touchscreen
Fully balanced analogue topology
Hybrid power mode
K2 + K2HD
Standard iFi digital filters
Bluetooth 5.4 with aptX Lossless, LDAC, LHDC, AAC, SBC
4.4mm + 3.5mm in/out
Same battery, same form factor, same power output
So, the core architecture is identical.
What the MT adds:
Upgraded analogue stage (Class A op‑amps, higher‑grade components, Audio Note Keisei capacitors)
Lower distortion and slightly cleaner midrange
Better separation and layering
Two exclusive Steve Levine filters (one PCM, one DSD)
Illuminated logo
A more “studio‑neutral” voicing compared to the warmer, more cinematic GR2
That’s it. No new DAC. No new Bluetooth chipset. No new power stage. No new screen. No new architecture.

And the price difference? 
GR2: £529
  /  
GR2 MT: £699

A £170 jump for what is essentially a “premium‑component edition” of the same device.

I’m not saying the MT is bad - it’s clearly a refinement, and I’m sure it sounds great. But the way this was released feels off. The GR2 came out, people bought it, settled in, and then just a couple of months later iFi drops a “Master Tuned” version with studio branding and a higher price tag. It’s hard not to feel like this was planned from the start and intentionally held back.

If you already own the GR2, here’s the honest truth: 
You still have 90–95% of the MT.
  The MT is not a GR3. It’s not a replacement. It’s not a new generation. It’s a refinement.

And depending on your listening preferences, the original GR2 might actually be the better match. The GR2 has a warmer, more musical, more cinematic presentation. The MT leans cleaner and more studio‑neutral. If you prefer warmth and body, the original GR2 is still the right choice.

But yes - the timing and positioning of the MT absolutely makes 
early GR2 buyers feel blindsided
. I’m one of them.

I’m happy with my GR2, but I’m not happy with how iFi handled this release.
